title: Brave Nazar
author: Hovhannes Tumanyan
short_summary: Nazar is the laziest, most cowardly man in his village. One night his wife shuts him out of the house, and in the morning he swats so many flies at once that he cannot count them — so he decides there must have been a thousand. A banner is written for him: "The invincible hero Brave Nazar, who with one blow smashes a thousand", and off the coward rides on his neighbour's donkey. One accident after another turns him into a hero, and then into a king, and nobody ever finds out the truth.
extended_summary:
Nazar is lazy, cowardly and boastful. One night his exasperated wife bolts the door on him, and he spends the night huddled against the wall. In the morning, with flies settling all over him, he strikes out with his hand and kills them. He cannot count the dead ones, so he decides there cannot have been fewer than a thousand. A banner is written: "The invincible hero Brave Nazar, who with one blow smashes a thousand." He fixes it to a stick, climbs onto his neighbour's donkey and rides off to conquer the world.

After that, everything is accident. Asleep up a tree in the forest, Nazar wakes to find a tiger lying beneath it, is so terrified that he falls out of the branches straight onto the animal's back, and clings on in horror — and everyone who sees it concludes that Brave Nazar rides tigers. Seven giant brothers who have heard of his fame accept him as their leader. In battle his horse bolts straight at the enemy, he grabs at a tree branch to steady himself, the branch snaps off in his hand, and the enemy — convinced he is advancing by tearing trees up by the roots — runs away.

Nazar is crowned. Nobody ever learns the truth: when people praise his courage and his cleverness he laughs and says it is all a matter of a man's luck, and he goes on reigning and laughing at the world.

questions.prompt: How does Nazar end up on the tiger's back?

options: He falls out of a tree onto it in fright
He mistakes it for his donkey in the dark
The seven brothers lift him onto the tiger
He catches it with a rope at the waterhole

questions.explanation: Nazar had gone to sleep up a tree, and the tiger lay down underneath it. He wakes, sees the animal, and is so frightened that he drops off the branch straight onto its back and clings on. The whole tale is built this way: every feat is an accident produced by terror.

questions.prompt: The words on Nazar's banner read: "The invincible hero Brave Nazar, who with one blow smashes a ___."
questions.explanation: The line sounds so impressive that nobody ever asks: a thousand what? That is the joke of the tale — a reputation is created by one sentence, and afterwards everyone bends what they see to fit it.

questions.prompt: Nazar kills the flies with one swat. Why does he decide there were a thousand of them?

options: He cannot count them, so he assumes no fewer
His wife counts them and tells him the number
A neighbour counts them and spreads the news
There really were a thousand: he counted carefully

questions.explanation: Nazar cannot manage to count the dead flies, so he picks the largest number that comes into his head. The lie does not start with wickedness — it starts with laziness and boasting, and then grows on its own.

questions.prompt: What does Nazar ride away on to conquer the world?

options: His neighbour's donkey
His own horse
A stallion given by the king
Nothing — he walks on foot

questions.explanation: Even the animal under him belongs to somebody else. The tale takes care to leave its hero owning nothing of his own — not courage, not strength, not so much as a donkey. All he has is the line on the banner.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of Nazar's rise to fame in the order they happen.

items: His wife bolts the door and he spends the night outside
In the morning he kills the flies with one blow
The two lines about him are written on a banner
Nazar rides off on his neighbour's donkey
Falling out of a tree, he lands on a tiger's back
In battle he routs the enemy with a broken branch

questions.explanation: Each step follows from the one before, and not one of them is a decision Nazar made. The tale shows fame as a rolling stone: pushed once, it keeps going, and every new accident gets explained by the reputation that already exists.

questions.prompt: Match each one to what they do in the story.

right: Throws him out of the house, then sends him into the world
Hear of his fame and accept him as their leader
Bolts in terror with a man clinging to its back
Runs away believing he uproots trees as he comes

questions.explanation: All four do more for Nazar than Nazar does. That is the tale's sharp point: the hero is manufactured by other people — a wife who has a banner written, onlookers who misread what they see, and an enemy who frightens itself.

questions.prompt: Sort each statement: is it what actually happened, or what people believed?

options.label: A frightened man fell out of a tree onto a beast
A horse bolted in terror towards the enemy
A snapped-off branch was left in his hand
Brave Nazar has tamed a tiger and rides it
He charges into battle first and without fear
He advances tearing trees up by the roots

questions.explanation: The three statements on each side are the same three moments, told twice. The tale is less about a liar than about how a crowd turns what it has seen with its own eyes into what it already believes.

questions.prompt: The enemy army runs away during the battle. What actually caused it?

options: A bolting horse and a broken branch in his hand
A secret attack by the seven brothers from behind
Nazar's loud and terrifying battle cry
The tiger, which came out onto the field with him

questions.explanation: His horse panics and charges straight at the enemy, Nazar snatches at a branch to hold on, and the branch breaks off in his hand. The enemy see a man hurtling towards them carrying an uprooted tree, and run. His greatest victory is pure terror, seen from the wrong side.

questions.prompt: Nazar becomes king without once doing anything brave. Did he deserve that throne? And if he did not, who is to blame for the fact that he got it? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both positions can earn full marks. A strong 'did not deserve it' answer notices that every feat was an accident — but the best answers go further and put some of the blame on the people who never checked. A strong 'deserved it' answer might argue that the enemy really was beaten and that the people got exactly what they wanted to believe. Accept any answer with a reason from the tale.

questions.prompt: Imagine that after he becomes king, Nazar is alone with you and admits that all of it came from fear and accidents. What would you tell him to do now, and why?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer gives concrete advice — confess, step down, actually learn to rule, surround himself with honest people — and says why that advice. A verdict like 'he is bad' with no advice attached is a weaker answer.

questions.prompt: Whenever people praise his courage and cleverness, Nazar laughs and answers that the whole thing is a matter of a man's ___.
questions.explanation: It is the slyest line in the tale: Nazar tells the plain truth, and precisely for that reason nobody believes him. It sounds like the modesty of a great man, and it is in fact a word-for-word confession.

questions.prompt: The seven giant brothers are far stronger than Nazar. Why do they accept him as their leader?

options: They believe the rumour and never think to test it
Nazar beats the strongest of them in single combat
He promises them half of all the future treasure
Their sister asks them to choose him as leader

questions.explanation: They are strong, but they have heard the line from the banner, and that is enough for them. The tale keeps making the same point: fear and rumour are stronger than truth wherever nobody dares to ask one simple question.
